question.questionText: We _______ in London for three years next week.
question.explanationHtml:
Detailed Explanation:
The blank requires the correct tense to express an action that will have lasted for a period of time by a specific point in the future. The phrase 'for three years next week' indicates a duration up to a future time. In English, the correct tense for this situation is the future perfect continuous tense: 'will have been + V-ing'. However, since 'live' is a stative verb and often used in the simple form, 'will have been' (future perfect) is commonly used with 'live' to indicate the duration up to a future point.
  • will be (verb phrase): Simple future tense, used for actions that will happen in the future, but does not express duration up to a future point.
  • will have been (verb phrase): Future perfect tense, used to show that something will have happened or been true for a period of time by a certain point in the future. Commonly used with stative verbs like 'live'.
  • will have (verb phrase): Future perfect tense, but incomplete without a past participle. Not correct in this context.
  • will have being (verb phrase): Incorrect form; 'being' is not used after 'will have'.
Related structure or vocabulary: Future perfect (will have + past participle) and future perfect continuous (will have been + V-ing) are used to express actions that will be completed or ongoing up to a point in the future. With stative verbs like 'live', 'will have been' is often used instead of the continuous form.
